WORKERS' COMPENSATION RETALIATION (LABOR CODE SECTION 132A) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Innovations LLC

INFORMATION AND BACKGROUND — ALLEGED WORKERS' COMPENSATION RETALIATION
I, Jordan Lee, am completing this information sheet in connection with my employment with Acme Innovations LLC. The workers' compensation-related activity I believe may be connected to an adverse action against me is described here as: Filed a workers' compensation claim on... The adverse action I believe may be connected to that activity is described here as: The employee was demoted and had their hours reduced within two weeks of filing a workers’ compensation claim., which I understand to have occurred on August 15, 2026.

This information sheet describes California Labor Code section 132a — a statute that separately prohibits certain kinds of employer and insurer conduct connected to a workers' compensation claim, and that is enforced through its own petition procedure before the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board rather than through a lawsuit filed in superior court. It is not a Labor Code section 132a petition, is not filed with the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board, any court, or any agency by completing it, and does not initiate any proceeding. Completing it does not establish that Jordan Lee was in fact discharged, threatened, or discriminated against by Acme Innovations LLC in violation of Labor Code section 132a, or that any specific fact stated here is true. Only the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board, or a court on judicial review of the appeals board's decision, can determine whether a violation of Labor Code section 132a occurred.

DECLARED POLICY AND THE CORE PROHIBITION — DISCHARGE, THREAT, OR DISCRIMINATION FOR A WORKERS' COMPENSATION CLAIM
California law declares it the policy of this state that there should not be discrimination against workers who are injured in the course and scope of their employment. Consistent with that declared policy, the same statute makes it a misdemeanor for an employer to discharge, threaten to discharge, or in any manner discriminate against an employee because the employee has filed or made known an intention to file a workers' compensation claim with the employer, or an application for adjudication, or because the employee has received a workers' compensation rating, award, or settlement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "It is the declared policy of this state that there should not be discrimination against workers who are injured in the course and scope of their employment."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 132a, declared policy (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=132a.)
  "Any employer who discharges, or threatens to discharge, or in any manner discriminates against any employee because he or she has filed or made known his or her intention to file a claim for compensation with his or her employer or an application for adjudication, or because the employee has received a rating, award, or settlement, is guilty of a misdemeanor"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 132a, paragraph (1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=132a.)
  Known gap: The two sentences quoted in this clause are the opening declaration and paragraph (1) of the same statutory section — Labor Code § 132a — not independent sources from each other; that is disclosed here rather than presented as two separate authorities. This is California's own statute, fetched directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and confirmed textually identical across two independent fetches using distinct User-Agent strings (a standard browser string and a distinct research-tool string); each quote in this clause was confirmed programmatically as an exact (whitespace-normalized) substring of that fetched text. Labor Code § 132a is enforced through a separate, Workers' Compensation Appeals Board-specific petition procedure addressed in a separate clause of this document — a genuinely distinct statutory scheme from Labor Code §§ 1102.5 and 98.6, the whistleblower and wage-claim retaliation statutes addressed in this corpus's separate Wrongful Termination in Violation of Public Policy information sheet, which are instead enforced through a civil action filed in superior court. No claim is made here about which of these statutes, if any, actually applies to a specific set of facts, or about which state's law governs a specific employment relationship. This document is informational: it does not itself determine that any specific discharge, threat, or discrimination occurred, that a specific employee's described adverse action was connected to the described activity, or that a violation of Labor Code § 132a occurred in this or any specific case.

A PARALLEL PROHIBITION ON INSURERS THAT PRESSURE AN EMPLOYER TO DISCHARGE
The same statute separately prohibits an insurer from advising, directing, or threatening an insured employer — under penalty of cancellation, a raise in premium, or for any other reason — to discharge an employee because the employee has filed or made known an intention to file a workers' compensation claim, or because the employee has received a rating, award, or settlement. An insurer that does so is guilty of a misdemeanor and is made subject to the same increased-compensation and cost remedy that applies to the employer's own violation of this statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]

  — Cal. Labor Code § 132a, paragraph (2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=132a.)

A SEPARATE PROTECTION — TESTIFYING, OR INTENDING TO TESTIFY, IN ANOTHER EMPLOYEE'S CASE
The same statute also separately makes it a misdemeanor for an employer to discharge, threaten to discharge, or in any manner discriminate against an employee because the employee testified, or made known an intention to testify, in another employee's case before the appeals board — a distinct category of prohibited conduct from the claim-filing protection addressed elsewhere in this document, and one that does not depend on the testifying employee having filed, or intending to file, any workers' compensation claim of their own. A parallel prohibition applies to an insurer that pressures an insured employer, under penalty of cancellation, a raise in premium, or for any other reason, to discharge or discriminate against an employee for that same reason.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]

  — Cal. Labor Code § 132a, paragraph (3) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=132a.)

  — Cal. Labor Code § 132a, paragraph (4) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=132a.)

THE REMEDY THIS STATUTE ITSELF AUTHORIZES — CURRENT DOLLAR AND PERCENTAGE FIGURES
For a violation of the claim-filing or rating/award/settlement-based prohibition, the statute itself increases the employee's workers' compensation by one-half, subject to a cap of ten thousand dollars, together with costs and expenses not exceeding two hundred fifty dollars; the same employee is also entitled to reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits caused by the employer's acts. This dollar and percentage structure was confirmed directly against the statute's own current, published text rather than assumed from an earlier or unverified figure.

FILED WITH THE WORKERS' COMPENSATION APPEALS BOARD — PETITION PROCEDURE AND ONE-YEAR TIME LIMIT
The statute itself states that proceedings for the increased-compensation remedy, or for reinstatement and reimbursement for lost wages and work benefits, are instituted by filing a petition with the Workers' Compensation Appeals Board — not by filing a civil action in superior court — and that these proceedings may not be commenced more than one year from the discriminatory act or the date the employee's employment was terminated. This document is informational: it does not itself file any petition, does not determine that any specific petition would be timely, properly pleaded, or successful, and does not determine that any violation of Labor Code § 132a occurred in this or any specific case.
